sections.html:
Roofing disputes rarely turn on whether a roof leaks. They turn on why it failed, when, who is responsible, and what a code-compliant repair costs. We answer those questions from field evidence, the building code adopted where the work was done, and the manufacturer's installation instructions, and we write them up so a mediator, appraisal panel, judge, or jury can follow the reasoning from photograph to conclusion.

  • Attorneys. Plaintiff and defense counsel in first-party property, bad faith, construction defect, subrogation, and jobsite injury matters.
  • Public adjusters. Independent field documentation and scope support on contested roof claims. We provide technical findings only and never adjust or negotiate the claim.
  • Insurance carriers. Claim professionals, independent adjusters, and coverage counsel who need a defensible inspection record or a review of a contractor scope.
  • Property managers and HOAs. Boards and managers facing multifamily roof failures, warranty disputes, or a decision about whether a defect claim is worth pursuing.

The side that retains us does not change the method. Fees are hourly or flat under a written retention agreement and never depend on the outcome.

Each service has its own page with methodology, deliverables, report format, and answers to common questions.

  • Expert roof inspections: forensic documentation of every slope, elevation, and detail, with measurements, layer counts, and chain of custody for anything removed.
  • Hail damage documentation: test squares, slope-by-slope counts, collateral indicators, and correlation with the recorded weather data for the dates at issue.
  • Cause and origin reports: written opinions separating hail, wind, mechanical damage, installation failure, age and wear, and foot traffic using a differential method.
  • Litigation support and expert witness: consulting and testifying roles, rebuttal review, demonstratives, deposition, and trial.
  • Appraisal and umpire support: measured scopes, line-item reconciliation, and code upgrade analysis for party appraisers and umpires.
  • Construction defect review: installation defects allocated among workmanship, product, and design, including Construction Defect Action Reform Act notice-of-claim inspections.
  • Fall protection standard of care: roofing jobsite falls reviewed against OSHA 29 CFR 1926 Subpart M and accepted roofing safety practice.

Not sure which applies? Call to talk through the questions in your matter. We run a conflict check before anything substantive is discussed.

1. Intake and conflict check. Send the parties, the property address, any insurers and contractors involved, and your deadlines. Do not send privileged material until the conflict check clears.
  2. Scoping call. A short call to define the questions, the record you have, the disclosure schedule, and whether you need a consulting expert, a testifying expert, or field documentation only.
  3. Retention. A written retention letter sets the role, the scope, and the fee basis. The fee schedule and CV are available on request.
  4. Records and inspection. We review the claim file, prior reports, permits, and weather record before going on the roof, then inspect with indexed photographs, measurements, and sampling under chain of custody where the parties agree.
  5. Report. Written findings and opinions tied to the adopted code, the manufacturer's instructions, and published industry references, formatted to support C.R.C.P. 26 or Fed. R. Civ. P. 26 disclosures.
  6. Testimony. Available for appraisal panels, mediation, arbitration, deposition, and trial.

Turnaround depends on access, weather, and the size of the record. We confirm at scoping whether we can meet your inspection and disclosure dates before accepting the engagement.

• Inspection report with dated, indexed photographs keyed to a roof diagram.
  • Standards analysis citing the adopted code section, manufacturer instruction, or OSHA provision behind each finding.
  • Weather and data correlation where timing is at issue, with the limits of each data source stated.
  • Line-item scope and estimate when cost is at issue, reconciled against competing estimates.
  • Rebuttal review of opposing expert reports, carrier scopes, and contractor estimates.
  • Testimony with demonstratives built from the field record.

Every report follows the same structure: executive summary, methodology, site observations, data correlation where relevant, analysis and opinions, limitations, and a photo appendix. Our opinions are roofing and construction opinions, not engineering opinions. When a question calls for a licensed professional engineer, such as structural capacity, we say so at scoping so counsel can retain one. We provide technical opinions, not legal advice.

We are based in Loveland and work statewide. Most engagements fall along the Front Range: Larimer, Weld, and Boulder counties, Longmont, and the Denver metro, where repeated hail seasons leave many roofs carrying marks from more than one storm. We also work in the mountain communities, including Estes Park, Grand County, Summit County, Eagle County, and Steamboat Springs, where storm reports are sparser, snow load and ice damming change the failure picture, and the physical evidence carries more weight. Travel is addressed in the retention letter.

Homeowners with a fresh storm claim should start with our hail damage repair and insurance claim roofing pages. The casualty practice is retained by counsel, carriers, adjusters, and appraisal panels, and a retained engagement is never combined with bidding, selling, or performing roofing work on the same property.

faq.q: Do you work for plaintiffs, defendants, or carriers?
faq.a: All three. We are retained by plaintiff and defense counsel, insurance carriers and their claim professionals, independent and public adjusters, and appraisers and umpires. The retaining party sets the questions, not the answers. The inspection method, the standards we cite, and the report structure are the same regardless of who engages us.

faq.q: What do you need to run a conflict check?
faq.a: The names of the parties, the property address, any insurers, contractors, or management companies involved, and your firm. That is enough to clear conflicts and disclose any prior relationship with the property. Please hold privileged documents until the conflict check clears and a retention letter is in place.

faq.q: Can you act as a public adjuster or negotiate a claim for a policyholder?
faq.a: No. Colorado law at C.R.S. 6-22-105 prohibits roofing contractors from acting as public adjusters, and we do not negotiate or settle claims for anyone. We provide independent technical findings to the party that retains us. Policyholders who want representation in their own claim should speak with a licensed public adjuster or an attorney.

faq.q: Are your reports engineering reports?
faq.a: No. Our opinions are roofing and construction opinions based on field inspection, the adopted building code, manufacturer installation instructions, and published industry practice. Where a question requires a licensed professional engineer, such as structural capacity, we flag it at scoping so counsel can retain the right discipline.

faq.q: How quickly can you inspect and report?
faq.a: It depends on roof access, weather, whether the inspection is joint with other parties, and the size of the record. At the scoping call we confirm whether we can meet your inspection date and disclosure deadline before we accept the engagement, and we tell you promptly if the schedule changes.

sections.h2: What a forensic roof inspection is
sections.html:
A forensic inspection differs from the free homeowner inspection we offer on the roofing side in purpose and in rigor. The homeowner inspection answers whether a roof needs work. The forensic inspection creates a record that can be produced in discovery, tested in deposition, and relied on by a trier of fact. That means a defined scope agreed with counsel, a repeatable photo protocol, measurements taken on the roof rather than estimated from a desk, and a written chain of custody for anything that leaves the property.

We inspect steep-slope asphalt shingle, tile, slate, cedar, synthetic, and metal roofs, and low-slope TPO, EPDM, PVC, and modified bitumen systems, on single-family, multifamily, HOA, and commercial buildings across Colorado. The inspection stands on its own or feeds a cause and origin report, a defect review, or an appraisal scope.

• Every slope and elevation. Overview photographs from the ground and the roof, then detail photographs of each condition with a scale, a direction reference, and a location on the roof diagram.
  • Measurements. Pitch by gauge on each slope, squares by slope, eave, rake, ridge, hip, and valley lengths, and roof height at the eave. Field numbers are checked against aerial measurement reports, not replaced by them.
  • Layers and deck. Number of roofing layers, underlayment type and laps where exposed, ice barrier extent, deck material and condition at any opening, and fastener type, count, and placement against the manufacturer's pattern.
  • Details. Step, counter, headwall, chimney, skylight, kick-out, and drip edge flashings, pipe boots, vents, intake and exhaust ventilation, gutters, and rooftop equipment.
  • Interior and attic. Staining, moisture readings, daylight at penetrations, ventilation paths, and insulation condition where access is safe and permitted.
  • Collateral surfaces. Soft metals, siding, screens, painted surfaces, and fences when hail or wind is a question, because they record size and direction.

Findings are tied to the edition of the International Residential Code (Chapter 9, including Section R905 roof covering requirements) or the International Building Code (Chapter 15) that the jurisdiction had adopted when the work was permitted, together with local amendments. Colorado adopts codes locally, so the governing edition in Fort Collins, Greeley, Boulder, Denver, or a mountain county can differ, and the report identifies which one applies.

Manufacturer installation instructions in effect at the time of installation are the second reference, because the code itself requires roof coverings to be installed per those instructions. Product classifications are cited where they matter: UL 2218 impact classes for hail resistance, ASTM D3161 and ASTM D7158 wind classifications for asphalt shingles, and the manufacturer's published slope and underlayment requirements.

Where samples or components are removed, removal is coordinated with all parties, photographed before and after, labeled, sealed, and logged. Openings are left weathertight. Where the question involves structural capacity, snow load calculations, or building science beyond roofing, we identify it at scoping so counsel can retain a licensed professional engineer.

Many inspections involve several parties on the roof at once. We draft or review the inspection protocol in advance: who attends, what areas are opened, how test cuts are sized and located, who photographs, how samples are split, and how the roof is restored. A protocol circulated before the inspection keeps the record clean and avoids disputes about spoliation later. For Construction Defect Action Reform Act notice-of-claim inspections, we attend for either side and document conditions and any destructive testing performed.

Ladder and fall protection on inspection days follow the same OSHA construction standards we cite in fall protection matters. Steep, high, icy, or brittle roofs are documented from the eave, a lift, or a drone where walking them is unsafe, and the report states which areas were observed directly and which were not.

Send the parties, the property address, and your deadlines for a conflict check. Once it clears, a short scoping call defines the questions and the inspection protocol, and a retention letter sets the role and fee basis. The fee schedule and CV are available on request. Turnaround depends on roof access, weather, and whether the inspection is joint, and we confirm at scoping whether we can meet your dates before accepting the engagement. We provide technical opinions, not legal advice, and we do not bid, sell, or perform roofing work on a property where we are retained as an expert.

faq.q: How is a forensic inspection different from a free roof inspection?
faq.a: A free homeowner inspection answers whether a roof needs work and what it would cost. A forensic inspection follows a scope agreed with counsel, uses a repeatable photo and measurement protocol, keeps chain of custody for anything removed, and produces a report formatted for disclosure and cross-examination. The retention letter sets the role before anyone goes on the roof.

faq.q: Will you attend a joint inspection with the other side's expert?
faq.a: Yes. We attend joint and multi-party inspections regularly and prefer a written protocol circulated beforehand that covers attendance, areas to open, test cut locations, photography, sample splitting, and restoration. That record protects every party against later disputes about what was observed or how the roof was left.

faq.q: Do you remove samples from the roof?
faq.a: When the scope calls for it and the parties agree. Removal is photographed before and after, each sample is labeled and sealed, and a chain-of-custody log records who handled it and when. Openings are repaired weathertight before we leave. Samples are retained or transferred as counsel directs.

faq.q: What if the roof is too steep or icy to walk?
faq.a: We document from the eave, a lift, or a drone and state in the report which slopes were observed directly and which were not. We do not walk roofs that cannot be walked safely under OSHA construction standards, and we will not represent an area as inspected when it was only viewed from a distance.

faq.q: Can the inspection report be used without a full expert report?
faq.a: Often, yes. Some matters need only a documented field record for a claim file, a mediation, or an appraisal panel. The inspection report stands alone with its photo appendix and measurement sheet, and can be expanded later into a cause and origin, defect, or cost opinion if the matter develops.

sections.html:
On the Front Range, many roofs have been through more than one hailstorm, and a dispute often hinges on a policy change, a prior paid claim, or a roof replaced between storms. The questions are whether hail damage is present, how much of it there is, whether it affects how the roof performs, and whether it matches the claimed date of loss. A field record that answers the first three cleanly is what makes the fourth answerable. Homeowners can read the basics in our guide to telling whether a roof has hail damage; this page describes the documentation product we deliver to counsel, adjusters, and carriers.

Our method follows published industry hail inspection protocols so the record can be reproduced and checked by the other side. The written causation opinion that draws on this record is described on the cause and origin reports page.

sections.h2: Test squares, chalk, and the photo protocol
sections.html:
• Test squares. Where it is safe, a 10 by 10 foot square is laid out on each directional slope, typically north, south, east, and west, plus any slope with a distinct exposure. Each square is chalked at the corners, photographed in overview with a scale, and then photographed mark by mark.
  • Marking. Hail-consistent marks are circled in chalk. Marks attributed to other causes, such as blisters, scuffs, nail pops, or mechanical damage, are marked with a different symbol so the photograph shows the distinction we drew in the field.
  • Photographs. Every detail photograph carries a scale, a slope and square reference, and a direction of view. Photographs are indexed to the roof diagram so any mark can be located again.
  • Beyond the squares. Ridge caps, hips, valleys, and soft metals are documented separately because they often show hail that field shingles do not, and because repairability depends on them.
  • Samples. When the parties agree, representative shingles or metal components are removed under chain of custody for later examination of fracture surfaces and granule displacement.

Counts are reported per square and per slope, never as a single number for the roof. Directional concentration is itself evidence: hail driven by storm wind marks the facing slopes harder, and a roof with uniform marks on every slope regardless of exposure is telling a different story than one with a clear directional pattern. The count table notes the type of mark observed, such as granule displacement with a fractured mat, a soft bruise without fracture, or a surface scuff, because the type bears on whether the damage is functional.

Collateral surfaces are surveyed and photographed on every elevation: soft metals on vents, flashings, and gutters, air conditioner condenser fins, window screens, siding, painted decks and fences, and vehicles if the owner permits. These surfaces record hail size and direction and help separate one storm from another. Oxidation and weathering inside dents and spatter marks are documented because they bear on timing.

The physical record is compared with the recorded weather for the property and the dates at issue. We use the NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information Storm Events Database, National Weather Service local storm reports, CoCoRaHS observer reports, and radar-derived hail products such as the Multi-Radar Multi-Sensor maximum estimated size of hail. Commercial hail swath reports are reviewed when produced by a party.

Each source has limits and the report states them. Storm Events and local storm reports depend on where observers happened to be. Radar products estimate hail aloft, not what reached a particular roof, and they can overstate or understate ground truth. We treat weather data as corroboration for the physical evidence, not a substitute for it. Where the data cannot separate two storms, the report says so rather than picking one. For the policyholder side of the question, see our note on whether homeowners insurance covers roof replacement in Colorado.

Policy language controls what is covered; we document the condition so the parties can apply it. The report distinguishes marks that fracture the shingle mat, displace granules to the asphalt, or puncture metal from marks that change appearance only. It also records shingle brittleness, the presence of a compatible replacement product, and local requirements such as UL 2218 Class 4 impact-resistant shingle mandates in some Larimer County jurisdictions, because those facts drive whether a repair or a replacement scope is realistic. Cost is addressed on the appraisal and umpire support page.

Send the parties, the property, the claimed date of loss, and your deadlines for a conflict check. Hail matters move faster when we see the claim file and the storm dates before going on the roof, so a short scoping call follows the conflict check. A retention letter sets the scope and fee basis; the fee schedule and CV are available on request. Turnaround depends on access and weather, and we confirm at scoping whether we can meet your dates. We are retained by counsel, carriers, adjusters, and appraisal panels. We do not handle claims for policyholders or act as a public adjuster.

faq.q: Do you use a 10 by 10 test square on every slope?
faq.a: Where it is safe to walk, yes, on each directional slope and on any slope with a distinct exposure. On slopes that cannot be walked safely, we document from the eave, a lift, or a drone and state that in the report. Test square locations are marked on the roof diagram so they can be found again.

faq.q: Is radar hail data enough to establish a date of loss?
faq.a: No. Radar products estimate hail in the storm, not what reached a specific roof, and ground reports depend on where observers were. We use NOAA Storm Events, National Weather Service reports, and radar estimates as corroboration alongside the physical evidence, and the report states where the data cannot separate two storms.

faq.q: How do you tell hail from blisters, scuffs, and nail pops?
faq.a: Hail-consistent marks are typically random, show displaced granules with a fractured mat or soft bruise beneath, and concentrate on slopes facing the storm. Blisters have raised, pitted edges, scuffs follow traffic paths, and nail pops sit on the fastener line. Each mark is classified in the field and chalked with a distinct symbol.

faq.q: What is the difference between functional and cosmetic hail damage?
faq.a: Functional damage reduces a roof's ability to shed water or shortens its service life, such as fractured shingle mats or punctured metal. Cosmetic damage changes appearance only, such as shallow dents in metal panels. Whether either is covered depends on the policy; we document the condition so the parties can apply the language.

faq.q: Can you document a roof that has already been replaced?
faq.a: Only from the record. If the roof is gone, we review prior inspection photographs, carrier and contractor photo sets, aerial imagery, permit records, and retained samples, and we say plainly which conclusions the surviving record supports and which it does not. Preserving a disputed roof or representative samples before replacement is strongly advisable.

sections.h2: What a cause and origin report answers
sections.html:
Leaks, blow-offs, cracked tiles, failed seams, and ice dam intrusion all have more than one possible cause, and the parties usually disagree about which one. The report answers four questions: what failed, what caused it, when the cause acted, and whether the failure is consistent with the claimed event. It is written so the opposing expert can follow the same evidence to test the conclusion, and so counsel can see where the opinion is strong and where it rests on a limited record.

The report draws on the field record described on the expert roof inspections and hail damage documentation pages, plus the claim file, permits, prior inspections, warranty records, and weather data.

• Hail. Random impact marks with displaced granules and fractured or bruised mat on shingles, fresh splits with impact marks on shakes, clean fractures on tile and slate, and sized, oriented dents on soft metals, concentrated on storm-facing slopes.
  • Wind. Creased, lifted, or missing shingles along the windward edges and at the ridge, broken sealant strips, exposed fastener lines, and uplift at membrane terminations, compared against the shingle's ASTM D3161 or D7158 wind class and the recorded gusts.
  • Mechanical damage. Ladder and tool marks, dents on faces hail could not reach, cuts and gouges from equipment, and damage grouped around service areas such as condensers and satellite mounts.
  • Installation failure. High, short, or over-driven fasteners, short laps, missing ice barrier, unsealed penetrations, absent kick-out flashing, and membrane seams that were never fully welded, measured against the manufacturer's instructions and the adopted code.
  • Age and wear. Uniform granule loss, thermal cracking, blistering, cupping and curling, sealant strip fatigue, and oxidation, accelerated on the Front Range by high-altitude UV and freeze-thaw cycling.
  • Foot traffic. Scuffs and crushed granules along paths between access points and rooftop equipment, broken tile at walkways, and membrane scuffing, often introduced during prior inspections or service calls.

Rather than looking for evidence of a preferred cause, we list every plausible cause for the observed condition, state the physical signature each cause would leave, and compare that signature to what is actually on the roof. Causes whose signatures are absent are ruled out with the reason stated. Causes whose signatures are present are weighed against each other, and the report explains why one is more consistent with the evidence than another. Where two causes are both consistent and the evidence cannot separate them, the report says that plainly.

The same discipline applies to timing. Weathering and oxidation at fracture surfaces and spatter marks, prior photographs, historical aerial imagery, permit history, and prior claims are compared with the recorded storm dates. The result is a date-of-loss opinion that states what the record supports rather than what either party hoped for.

Opinions are tied to the International Residential Code Chapter 9 or International Building Code Chapter 15 edition and local amendments in force when the roof was permitted, the manufacturer's installation instructions in effect at the time, and product classifications such as UL 2218 impact classes. Weather sources are identified with their limits stated.

Colorado courts admit expert testimony under Colorado Rule of Evidence 702 and the standard set in People v. Shreck, which asks whether the underlying principles are reasonably reliable, whether the witness is qualified, and whether the testimony will help the trier of fact, subject to Rule 403. Federal courts apply Rule 702 and Daubert. A differential method with stated reasoning and stated limits is written with those inquiries in mind. Reports are formatted to support C.R.C.P. 26 and Fed. R. Civ. P. 26 expert disclosures. Whether a method satisfies the standard in a given case is for the court; we provide technical opinions, not legal advice.

Send the parties, the property, the claimed event, and your deadlines for a conflict check. A scoping call then defines the questions and the record, and a retention letter sets the role as consulting or testifying expert. The fee schedule, CV, and any prior testimony disclosures the rules require are available on request. Turnaround depends on the record and site access, and we confirm feasibility at scoping. A retained engagement is never combined with bidding, selling, or performing roofing work on the same property.

faq.q: Can you tell which of two storms caused the damage?
faq.a: Often we can narrow it by comparing weathering, oxidation, and fracture freshness with recorded storm dates, reported hail sizes, prior photographs, and aerial imagery. Sometimes the evidence genuinely cannot separate two events, and the report says so. An opinion that overstates what the record supports does not survive cross-examination.

faq.q: What does a differential method mean in a roofing report?
faq.a: It means listing every plausible cause of the observed condition, stating the physical signature each would leave, and comparing those signatures to the roof. Causes whose signatures are absent are ruled out with the reason stated. Remaining causes are weighed against each other and the report explains why one is more consistent than another.

faq.q: Will the opinion hold up under Rule 702?
faq.a: Admissibility is decided by the court, not by us. What we control is the method: field observation, stated standards, a reasoning chain the other side can test, and limits stated plainly. Colorado applies the Shreck reliability and relevance inquiry under CRE 702; federal courts apply Daubert. Reports are written with both in mind.

faq.q: Do you give coverage opinions?
faq.a: No. We document the condition, the cause, and the timing. Whether a cause or a type of damage is covered depends on the policy language and Colorado law, which are questions for counsel and the trier of fact. Our reports distinguish functional from cosmetic damage so the parties can apply the policy terms themselves.

faq.q: Can you address wind and hail on the same roof?
faq.a: Yes. Wind and hail leave different signatures and often arrive in the same storm. The report addresses each cause separately, maps where each appears on the roof, and compares wind findings with the shingle's rated wind class and the recorded gusts, so the parties can see what portion of the condition each cause explains.

sections.html:
Many engagements start as consulting work so counsel can evaluate the roofing issues before deciding whether to disclose an expert. In a consulting role we review the record, inspect if needed, and give candid feedback on the strengths and weaknesses of the technical case. If the matter proceeds, the role can convert to testifying under the same retention letter, with the report and disclosures prepared to the applicable rules. The role is set in writing at retention and can change as the case develops.

Engagements cover residential, multifamily, HOA, and commercial buildings with asphalt shingle, tile, slate, cedar, synthetic, metal, and low-slope membrane roofs across Colorado.

sections.h2: The roofing questions behind the case
sections.html:
• Cause of loss. Hail, wind, age, installation error, or product failure, and whether the damage matches the claimed date of loss. See cause and origin reports.
  • Construction defect. Whether the work followed the adopted code and manufacturer instructions, and whether a failure traces to workmanship, product, or design. See construction defect review.
  • Standard of care. Whether a roofing contractor, general contractor, or site supervisor met code, OSHA 1926 Subpart M, and accepted industry practice. See fall protection standard of care.
  • Cost and scope. What a code-compliant repair or replacement includes and what it reasonably costs in the local market. See appraisal and umpire support.
  • Claim-handling facts. In matters brought under C.R.S. 10-3-1115 and 10-3-1116, which address unreasonable delay or denial of a first-party claim, we can address what a reasonable roof inspection would have documented and whether a scope omitted code-required or manufacturer-required items. Whether a carrier acted without a reasonable basis is a question for counsel and the trier of fact.

Colorado courts evaluate expert testimony under Colorado Rule of Evidence 702 and People v. Shreck, a reliability and relevance inquiry that considers the totality of the circumstances, the qualifications of the witness, and whether the testimony will help the trier of fact, balanced against Rule 403. Federal courts apply Rule 702 and Daubert. Both inquiries reward the same things: a method the other side can follow, standards cited by section, observations separated from inferences, and limits stated rather than hidden.

Reports are prepared to support C.R.C.P. 26(a)(2) and Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(a)(2) disclosures, including the materials considered, the compensation basis, and prior testimony where the rules require it. We keep working notes, field data, and photographs in a form that can be produced.

Rebuttal review takes an opposing report, carrier scope, or contractor estimate line by line and classifies each disagreement as a difference in observation, measurement, standard applied, or pricing. That structure lets counsel see which disputes are factual and which are judgment calls. Demonstratives are built from the field record: annotated photographs, roof diagrams with test square or defect locations, layered detail drawings, and side-by-side comparison tables.

We are available for deposition, mediation, arbitration, appraisal panel presentations, and trial. Testimony is explained in plain language a jury can follow from photograph to conclusion without losing the technical foundation.

sections.h2: Statutes that shape Colorado roofing disputes
sections.html: Counsel will know these; we cite them here because they frame the technical questions we are asked. C.R.S. 6-22-105 prohibits roofing contractors from paying, waiving, or rebating deductibles and from acting as public adjusters. C.R.S. 10-3-1115 and 10-3-1116 address unreasonable delay or denial of first-party benefits and provide for recovery of two times the covered benefit plus fees and costs. C.R.S. 13-80-104 sets the limitation and repose periods for construction claims, and the Construction Defect Action Reform Act at C.R.S. 13-20-801 and following sets the notice-of-claim process. OSHA 29 CFR 1926 Subpart M governs fall protection in construction. How each applies to a given matter is a legal question; our role is the technical record beneath it.

Our opinions follow the evidence. We do not take contingency fees on expert work, we do not bid, sell, or perform roofing work on a property where we are retained, and we disclose any prior relationship with the property or parties at intake. Send the parties, the property, and your deadlines for a conflict check. A scoping call follows, then a retention letter setting the role and fee basis. The fee schedule, CV, and prior testimony list are available on request. Turnaround is confirmed at scoping against your disclosure schedule. We provide technical opinions, not legal advice.

faq.q: Can you serve as a consulting expert, a testifying expert, or both?
faq.a: Yes. Many engagements begin as consulting so counsel can evaluate the technical case before deciding whether to disclose us. The role is set in the written retention letter and can convert to testifying as the case develops, with the report and disclosures prepared to the applicable rules.

faq.q: Do you provide a CV, fee schedule, and prior testimony disclosures?
faq.a: Yes. A CV and fee schedule are provided on request, along with the prior testimony list the rules require. Reports are prepared to support C.R.C.P. 26 and Fed. R. Civ. P. 26 expert disclosures, including materials considered and the compensation basis.

faq.q: Will you review the other side's expert report?
faq.a: Yes. Rebuttal review works line by line and classifies each disagreement as a difference in observation, measurement, standard applied, or pricing. Where the opposing expert is right on a point, we say so, because a rebuttal that disputes everything is not useful to counsel or credible to a trier of fact.

faq.q: Do you give legal advice or coverage opinions?
faq.a: No. We provide technical opinions about roofs, construction, and jobsite practice. Coverage, liability, reasonableness of claim handling, and damages are questions for counsel and the trier of fact. We can describe what a reasonable inspection would have documented and what a code-compliant scope includes.

faq.q: Where in Colorado do you testify?
faq.a: Statewide. Most matters arise along the Front Range from Fort Collins and Greeley through Boulder, Longmont, and the Denver metro, with regular work in the mountain communities. Travel for inspections, depositions, and trial is addressed in the retention letter.

faq.q: Are you an engineer?
faq.a: No, and our reports say so. Our opinions are roofing and construction opinions grounded in field inspection, the adopted code, manufacturer instructions, and industry practice. Where a question requires a licensed professional engineer, such as structural capacity or snow load, we flag it at scoping so counsel can retain one.

sections.html:
Most property policies let either party demand appraisal when they disagree on the amount of loss. Each side selects an appraiser, the appraisers select an umpire, and agreement by any two sets the amount. The Colorado Supreme Court has held that an appraiser must be impartial: neutral, without a stake in the result, and not an advocate for the party who selected them, although an appraiser may defend a methodology or data choice when the aim is an accurate result. Whether an appraisal panel may decide causation or coverage, and how the award is enforced, depend on the policy language and Colorado law and are questions for counsel.

Our role is technical. We supply the panel, a party appraiser, or an umpire with a measured, documented scope and a reconciliation that shows exactly where and why the competing numbers differ. Where the policy and the parties permit, we can serve as a party-selected appraiser on roofing losses, subject to the same impartiality obligation and full disclosure of any prior relationship with the property or parties.

A defensible number starts with quantities someone measured. We take measurements on the roof, record layers, deck condition, and existing details, and check the field numbers against aerial measurement reports rather than replacing them. The scope is then built in the line-item format carriers and contractors use, including Xactimate, so it reconciles directly against the estimates already in the file.

  • Quantities. Squares by slope, pitch, waste factor, and ridge, hip, valley, eave, and rake lengths.
  • Tear-off and disposal by layer, including additional layers found in the field.
  • Components. Flashings, vents, pipe boots, skylights, gutters, and detach and reset of solar arrays and rooftop equipment.
  • Access and safety. Steep and high charges, fall protection, staging, and mountain access.
  • Project costs. Permits, sales tax at the local rate, and general contractor overhead and profit where the scope reasonably requires a general contractor.

Prices reflect the local market at the valuation date counsel or the panel specifies, with sources recorded so they can be tested. Homeowners can read how to interpret a scope in our guide to reading a roofing estimate.

Most appraisal disputes are resolved line by line, not in the total. The reconciliation table lines up our scope against each competing estimate and classifies every difference as quantity, unit price, or scope, with a one-line explanation. Common disputes include waste factors on cut-up roofs, whether a repair can meet the manufacturer's instructions on brittle shingles, whether a compatible product is still available, steep and high charges, overhead and profit, detach and reset of rooftop equipment, and the treatment of ridge, hip, and starter courses. Each is addressed with a photograph, a measurement, or a cited instruction rather than an assertion.

Items the adopted code requires that were not present before the loss are identified, cited to the code section and any local amendment, and priced separately so the parties can apply the policy's ordinance or law terms. Typical items on the Front Range include ice barrier at eaves and valleys, drip edge, underlayment type, ventilation balance, and UL 2218 Class 4 impact-resistant shingles where a jurisdiction mandates them. Because Colorado adopts codes locally, the schedule identifies the edition and amendments in force for the specific jurisdiction and permit date.

We are retained by attorneys, carriers, and appraisers or umpires to provide independent technical scopes. We do not represent policyholders, negotiate or settle claims, or act as a public adjuster. C.R.S. 6-22-105 prohibits roofing contractors from paying, waiving, or rebating any part of a deductible and from acting as public adjusters; our estimates never assume a waived deductible, and a retained casualty engagement is never combined with bidding, selling, or performing the work on the same property. Policyholders looking for help with their own claim should speak with a licensed public adjuster or an attorney, and can read our insurance claim roofing page for how the process works on the contractor side.

Tell us the parties, the property, the valuation date, and who the scope is for at intake, because all three shape the work. After the conflict check and a scoping call, a retention letter sets the role, which may be technical consultant to an appraiser or umpire, party-selected appraiser where permitted, or expert for counsel. The fee schedule and CV are available on request, and fees never depend on the outcome. Turnaround is confirmed at scoping against the panel's schedule. We provide technical opinions, not legal advice.

faq.q: Can you serve as a party-appointed appraiser?
faq.a: Where the policy and the parties permit, yes, on roofing losses. A party-selected appraiser in Colorado must be impartial, without a stake in the result, and must not advocate for the selecting party. We disclose any prior relationship with the property or parties at intake, and the fee is hourly or flat, never contingent on the award.

faq.q: Do you price at the date of loss or at today's prices?
faq.a: Whichever the matter requires. Counsel or the panel specifies the valuation date, and we document the pricing sources for that date so the numbers can be checked. Where both dates matter, the estimate can be run at each with the difference shown line by line.

faq.q: Will you negotiate with the insurance company for a homeowner?
faq.a: No. Colorado law at C.R.S. 6-22-105 prohibits roofing contractors from acting as public adjusters, and we do not negotiate or settle claims for anyone. We provide independent technical scopes to the party that retains us. Homeowners who want representation should speak with a licensed public adjuster or an attorney.

faq.q: Do you include code upgrade items?
faq.a: Yes. Each code-required item that was not present before the loss is cited to the adopted code section and local amendment for the specific jurisdiction and priced separately. That lets the parties apply the policy's ordinance or law terms without reworking the estimate.

faq.q: Can you review the other side's estimate without inspecting?
faq.a: A desk review can flag missing items, measurement inconsistencies, and pricing outside the local market, and the report states that it is based on the file alone. Where quantities are disputed, a site measurement resolves the question faster than two desk estimates arguing about aerial reports.

sections.html:
We review steep-slope shingle, tile, slate, cedar, synthetic, and metal roofs, and low-slope TPO, EPDM, PVC, and modified bitumen systems on single-family, multifamily, HOA, and commercial projects. The conditions that generate claims are predictable.

  • Underlayment and ice barrier. Type, laps, and extent at eaves, valleys, walls, and penetrations against International Residential Code Section R905 and the manufacturer's requirements.
  • Fastening. Nail type, count, placement, and depth against the manufacturer's pattern; high, short, angled, and over-driven fasteners.
  • Flashing. Step, counter, headwall, chimney, skylight, kick-out, and drip edge details, and the sequencing with the wall cladding and weather-resistive barrier.
  • Ventilation. Intake and exhaust balance and its effect on ice dams, condensation, shingle service life, and warranty coverage.
  • Low-slope membranes. Seam welds, terminations, flashings at curbs and walls, drainage, crickets, and ponding.
  • Transitions. Roof-to-wall intersections, deck-to-wall ledgers, and the details where roofing meets siding, stucco, or masonry.

Allocation often decides a defect case, and each source leaves a different pattern. Workmanship is installation that departs from the manufacturer's instructions or the adopted code: high nails, short laps, missing kick-out flashing, unsealed penetrations, unwelded seams. It usually repeats wherever the same crew did the same detail the same way. Product failures appear across the roof regardless of technique: widespread blistering, sealant strip failure, factory seam defects, premature granule loss. We record lot numbers, packaging, and warranty registration where available. Design defects are details that cannot perform as drawn: inadequate slope on low-slope areas, missing crickets behind wide chimneys, valleys discharging against walls, ventilation that cannot balance. Questions involving structure or building science beyond roofing are flagged for the appropriate licensed professional.

1. Document review. Plans, specifications, submittals, permits and inspection records, warranty registrations, daily logs, change orders, and the manufacturer's installation instructions in effect when the roof was installed.
  2. Non-destructive survey. Every slope and detail photographed and mapped, with moisture readings and controlled water testing where they help locate an entry point.
  3. Destructive testing. Test cuts and tear-backs under a protocol agreed by the parties. Each layer is photographed and measured, samples are preserved under chain of custody, and openings are left weathertight.
  4. Code analysis. Findings tied to the IRC Chapter 9 or IBC Chapter 15 edition and local amendments the jurisdiction had adopted when the work was permitted, not today's code, together with the manufacturer's instructions and any product evaluation reports.
  5. Repair scope. A repair that fixes the defect without overreaching, priced line by line, with access, staging, and code-required work included. See appraisal and umpire support for the estimating method.

Colorado's Construction Defect Action Reform Act, C.R.S. 13-20-801 and following, generally requires a claimant to give a construction professional written notice before filing suit, with an opportunity to inspect and to offer to repair or settle. We attend and document notice-of-claim inspections for either side, evaluate proposed repairs, and prepare defect and repair-cost opinions.

C.R.S. 13-80-104 sets a two-year limitation period running from when the claimant discovered or should have discovered the physical manifestation of the defect, and a six-year repose period from substantial completion, extended to eight years for a defect discovered in the fifth or sixth year. House Bill 25-1272, signed in May 2025 and effective August 6, 2025, changed the owner approval threshold for common interest community boards bringing defect claims and created an optional warranty and inspection program for builders. Deadlines, thresholds, and procedure are for counsel; our role is the technical record. For a related question on the insurance side, see whether homeowners insurance covers roof replacement.

Defect matters often involve several parties and a destructive testing protocol, so we plan the inspection with counsel before anyone goes on the roof. Send the parties, the project, the roles, and your deadlines for a conflict check. A scoping call follows, then a retention letter and, where needed, a testing protocol circulated to the parties. The fee schedule and CV are available on request. Turnaround depends on records, access, and coordination among parties, and we confirm feasibility at scoping. We provide technical opinions, not legal advice, and we never bid or perform the repair on a property where we are retained.

faq.q: How do you tell a workmanship defect from a product defect?
faq.a: By pattern and by evidence under the surface. Workmanship defects follow the installer and repeat at the same details. Product defects appear across the roof regardless of technique. We open representative areas, measure what was installed against the manufacturer's pattern, and record product lot information and warranty registration where available.

faq.q: Which code edition applies to the roof?
faq.a: The edition and local amendments the jurisdiction had adopted when the work was permitted, together with the manufacturer's installation instructions in effect at that time. Colorado adopts codes locally, so the answer differs between cities and counties. The report identifies both the edition and the amendments relied on.

faq.q: Can you attend a CDARA notice-of-claim inspection?
faq.a: Yes, for either side. We document conditions and any destructive testing, evaluate a proposed repair against the defects observed, and prepare a written opinion. We provide technical opinions only; CDARA deadlines, notice requirements, and procedure are questions for counsel.

faq.q: Do you perform destructive testing?
faq.a: When the parties agree on a protocol. We photograph and measure each layer as it is exposed, preserve samples under a chain-of-custody log, and leave every opening weathertight. The protocol is circulated before the inspection so no party is surprised by what is opened or how.

faq.q: Do you review multifamily and commercial roofs?
faq.a: Yes. We review single-family, multifamily, HOA, and commercial buildings, including steep-slope shingle, tile, slate, cedar, and metal roofs and low-slope TPO, EPDM, PVC, and modified bitumen systems. Large projects are sampled under a documented plan so the findings can be extrapolated with the method stated.

faq.q: Can you price the repair?
faq.a: Yes. We prepare line-item repair scopes and estimates tied to the defects identified, including access, staging, permits, and code-required work. The scope is written to fix the defect without overreaching, and it reconciles line by line against any competing repair estimate in the file.

sections.h2: Was the fall foreseeable and preventable
sections.html:
Roofing falls are rarely a single failure. They usually involve a plan that did not match the roof, equipment that was missing or rigged wrong, or supervision that did not enforce what the safety program required. We reconstruct what was planned, what was provided, and what was used, and compare it to the OSHA construction standards and to accepted practice on Colorado residential and commercial roofs.

  • Planning. Site-specific safety and fall protection plans, and whether they fit the roof's height, slope, and width.
  • Equipment. Anchors, lifelines, harnesses, lanyards, guardrails, warning lines, hole covers, and ladders: what was provided and how it was rigged.
  • Training and supervision. Fall protection training under 29 CFR 1926.503 and competent person oversight.
  • Site control. Who controlled the site and the means and methods among owner, general contractor, roofer, and subcontractors.
  • Conditions. Frost, snow, wet membranes, wind, skylights, brittle decking, and access points.

sections.h2: OSHA 1926 Subpart M in plain terms
sections.html:
A general summary of the federal construction fall protection standards. Colorado private-sector construction is enforced by federal OSHA rather than a state plan.

  • Six-foot trigger. In construction, fall protection is generally required when a worker is exposed to a fall of 6 feet or more to a lower level, under 29 CFR 1926.501(b)(1).
  • Low-slope roofs. On roofs of 4 in 12 or less, 1926.501(b)(10) allows guardrails, safety nets, personal fall arrest, or a warning line system combined with one of those or a safety monitor. A safety monitoring system alone is limited to roofs 50 feet or less in width.
  • Steep roofs. On roofs steeper than 4 in 12, 1926.501(b)(11) requires guardrails with toeboards, safety nets, or personal fall arrest systems.
  • Residential construction. Under 1926.501(b)(13), conventional fall protection is required at 6 feet unless the employer demonstrates it is infeasible or creates a greater hazard, in which case a written, site-specific fall protection plan meeting 1926.502(k) is required. OSHA directive STD 03-11-002 governs enforcement, and slide guards alone do not satisfy the rule.
  • Holes and skylights. Workers must be protected from falling through holes, including skylights, by covers, guardrails, or personal fall arrest under 1926.501(b)(4).
  • Systems and training. 1926.502 sets system criteria such as anchorage strength, guardrail dimensions, and warning line placement; 1926.503 requires training by a competent person; ladders fall under Subpart X.

sections.h2: How we investigate a roofing fall
sections.html:
Scene documentation. Eave and ridge heights, slope by pitch gauge, roof width, anchor locations and substrate, access points, hole and skylight locations, and the surface condition at the fall location, all photographed and measured. Equipment and custody. Harnesses, lanyards, lifelines, anchors, and ladders are inspected, labels and serial numbers recorded, and items held under a chain-of-custody log when the parties ask. Records review. Safety programs, fall protection plans, job hazard analyses, toolbox talk and training records, daily logs, subcontracts allocating safety duties, and any OSHA inspection file produced.

Standard of care reaches beyond the regulation text to the manufacturer's instructions for fall protection equipment, consensus standards such as ANSI/ASSP Z359, and common practice on Colorado residential and commercial roofs. Where responsibility among several employers is at issue, we explain how OSHA's multi-employer citation policy describes creating, exposing, correcting, and controlling employers, and how site control was actually exercised. Early contact matters most in fall cases because equipment and site conditions change quickly. The same field discipline applies to our expert roof inspections.

Plaintiff and defense counsel in personal injury and wrongful death matters, and carriers and counsel in subrogation and third-party matters related to workers' compensation where the jobsite safety facts are disputed. Falls happen on Front Range reroofs, new multifamily construction, and mountain projects where snow, ice, and steep pitches raise the stakes. An OSHA citation does not by itself establish negligence, and the absence of one does not establish that the work was safe; how the regulations bear on the standard of care is a legal question for counsel and the court. We explain what the regulations require, what industry practice is, and what the evidence shows was done. Related: construction defect review and litigation support.

Preserve the harness, lanyard, anchor, ladder, and any photographs of the edge and anchors as they were, then send the parties, the site, the date, and your deadlines for a conflict check. A scoping call follows, with guidance on preserving equipment and site conditions under chain of custody, then a retention letter setting the role and fee basis. The fee schedule and CV are available on request. Turnaround is confirmed at scoping against your schedule. We provide technical opinions, not legal advice.

faq.q: When is fall protection required on a roof?
faq.a: Under OSHA's construction standards, generally whenever a worker is exposed to a fall of 6 feet or more to a lower level. The acceptable systems depend on whether the roof is low-slope or steep, whether the work is residential construction under 1926.501(b)(13), and whether holes or skylights are present.

faq.q: Is a safety monitor enough on a residential reroof?
faq.a: Usually not by itself. A safety monitoring system alone is an option only for low-slope roofs 50 feet or less in width. On residential work, OSHA expects guardrails, safety nets, or personal fall arrest unless the employer shows those are infeasible or create a greater hazard and follows a written site-specific plan under 1926.502(k).

faq.q: Does an OSHA citation prove negligence?
faq.a: Not by itself, and the absence of a citation does not prove the work was safe. How OSHA regulations bear on the standard of care is a legal question for counsel and the court. We explain what the regulations require, what accepted roofing practice is, and what the evidence shows was actually done on the site.

faq.q: What evidence matters most after a roofing fall?
faq.a: The equipment itself, photographs of the roof edge and anchors as they were, the fall protection plan, training records, subcontracts allocating safety duties, and witness accounts of how the crew was tied off. Preserve the harness, lanyard, and anchor before anything is reused, repaired, or discarded, and record who has handled them.

faq.q: Can you evaluate the general contractor's role as well as the roofer's?
faq.a: Yes. We review contracts, site control, the safety program, and supervision to show how responsibility was set up and carried out on the site, and we explain how OSHA's multi-employer citation policy describes creating, exposing, correcting, and controlling employers. Allocation of legal responsibility remains a question for counsel and the court.
